items.title: Liquid-biopsy methylation panel for early colorectal cancer detection
items.summary: A 12-marker plasma panel that detects stage I–II disease from a standard blood draw.
items.problem: Most colorectal cancers in the target population are diagnosed at stage III–IV, and adherence to colonoscopy screening stays below 40%. A blood-based triage test was needed to decide who should be referred first.
items.method: Targeted bisulfite sequencing of cell-free DNA in 412 plasma samples from two hospitals, with a pre-registered case-control design. Candidate regions were ranked by a regularised classifier and locked before testing on a held-out set.
items.role: Scientific lead: study design, wet-lab protocol, analysis plan and supervision of a four-person team.
items.impact: The locked panel reached an AUC of 0.93, with 87% sensitivity at 92% specificity for stage I–II disease. A PCT application was filed and the assay moved to a diagnostics partner for analytical validation.

items.title: Patient-derived organoid platform for drug-response profiling
items.summary: A standardised organoid biobank and assay set that predicts chemotherapy response before treatment.
items.problem: Two-dimensional cell lines predict clinical response poorly, which contributes to attrition rates above 90% in oncology development. Partners needed a model closer to the patient that could still run at screening throughput.
items.method: Established 38 gastric and colorectal organoid lines with matched clinical data. Viability and high-content imaging assays were standardised in 384-well format under GLP-aligned SOPs, with plate-level quality criteria (Z′ > 0.7).
items.role: Platform owner: protocol development, assay validation, SOP authoring and training of three partner groups.
items.impact: Screening turnaround fell from 6 to 2.5 weeks. In a retrospective set of 22 patients, organoid response agreed with clinical response in 82% of cases. Three external groups adopted the protocol.

items.title: Multi-omics host signature predicting severe dengue
items.summary: An 8-gene signature, measured in the first 72 hours of fever, that flags patients likely to progress.
items.problem: During outbreaks, clinicians cannot tell early which dengue patients will develop severe disease, so hospitals admit far more people than need care. No validated early predictor was available.
items.method: Integrated whole-blood RNA-seq and targeted plasma proteomics from 186 patients. All steps run in a containerised Nextflow pipeline, and the signature was tested in an independent cohort of 94 patients from a different region.
items.role: Lead analyst and work-package co-lead: analysis strategy, pipeline architecture and external validation.
items.impact: The signature reached an AUC of 0.89 in external validation. The pipeline is open source and has been reused by five laboratories. The signature is the basis for an RT-qPCR prototype now under licence.

items.title: Companion-diagnostic assay for an immuno-oncology asset
items.summary: A stratification assay developed and transferred ahead of a sponsor's Phase II start.
items.problem: A biopharma sponsor needed a patient-stratification assay in place before starting Phase II, with a fixed regulatory timeline and no validated method available.
items.method: Design-of-experiments optimisation of a multiplex immunoassay under ISO 13485-aligned design control, followed by analytical validation against pre-specified acceptance criteria and a full technology-transfer package.
items.role: Project lead for a six-person cross-functional team, and main scientific contact for the sponsor.
items.impact: All pre-specified acceptance criteria were met, with inter-run variability under 10%. The package was delivered 4–6 weeks ahead of plan and transferred to the sponsor's contract laboratory without re-development.

items.title: Plasma cell-free DNA methylation signatures enable early-stage colorectal cancer detection in a Latin American cohort
items.authors: Medina-Ortiz K, Ramírez J, Duarte P, Henao M, Castaño L
items.tldr: A blood test based on 12 DNA marks detects early colorectal cancer with accuracy close to current screening tools. It could prioritise who needs a colonoscopy.

items.title: An integrated transcriptomic and proteomic signature predicts progression to severe dengue
items.authors: Medina-Ortiz K*, Salazar A*, Okafor N, Vélez D, Brandt H
items.tldr: Eight genes measured in the first three days of fever identify patients at risk of severe dengue. Validated in an independent cohort from another region.

items.title: Standardised patient-derived organoid assays predict chemotherapy response in gastric cancer
items.authors: Medina-Ortiz K, Lemaire C, Pardo S, Giraldo F, Castaño L
items.tldr: Mini-tumours grown from patient biopsies responded to drugs the same way the patients did in 82% of cases. The protocol runs at screening scale.

items.title: A reproducible Nextflow workflow for multi-omics integration in small clinical cohorts
items.authors: Salazar A, Brandt H, Medina-Ortiz K
items.tldr: An open-source pipeline that lets small clinical teams combine several data types reliably. Results can be re-run and audited by a third party.

items.title: Circulating microRNA profiles as minimally invasive markers of treatment response in gastric cancer
items.authors: Medina-Ortiz K, Henao M, Duarte P, Castaño L
items.tldr: Small RNA molecules in blood shift within weeks when chemotherapy is working. They offer an earlier signal than imaging for adjusting treatment.

items.title: Tumour–stroma crosstalk shapes drug tolerance in three-dimensional co-culture models
items.authors: Lemaire C, Pardo S, Medina-Ortiz K, et al.
items.tldr: Supporting cells around a tumour help it tolerate drugs. Including them in lab models gives a more realistic picture of drug efficacy.

about.title: A scientist who builds things other teams can use
bio: I trained as a biologist in Colombia and completed a PhD in Biomedical Sciences focused on translational oncology. My work sits between discovery and development: finding signals in patient samples, proving they hold up, and packaging them so a partner can take them further.
I work in English, Spanish and French, and I am comfortable presenting to clinicians, investors and regulators as well as to other scientists.
